title.en: Cloth display motion versus mass-spring simulation

summary: Compare an authored textile display with a selected particle-spring example; other declared cloth formulations remain valid, and neither example establishes tested fabric properties.
objective: Choose an authored textile display or the selected mass-spring sheet example; inspect pinned particles and report stretch against a declared tolerance without treating spring families as a hard bound.
applies_when: A flag, curtain, garment or banner is asked to move, hang or collide.
The user might read the motion as physical drape rather than decoration.
example_prompts: Hang a sheet from two corners with visible structural, shear and bend springs.
Wave a banner with an authored clip and label it as display, not a cloth solver.
negative_signals: Vertex shader ripples claimed as drape prediction.
A skinned cloak clip presented as collision response.
not_for: Laboratory fabric identification, measured drape coefficients or cutting-pattern CAD.
Continuum shell finite elements, which this record does not specify.

principles: This record compares authored display with one discrete mass-spring formulation. Other cloth solvers and explicitly coordinated hybrids remain valid choices.
The selected sheet owns particles and structural, shear and flexion springs. These are modeling elements, not measured textile properties or a universal requirement for cloth.
Large local extensions can be an artifact of this elastic formulation. Selecting spring families does not by itself enforce maximum stretch.
implementation: Display branch: own clip, morph or shader state. Describe pins or gravity only as authored appearance unless they actually enter a solver.

Simulation branch: own particle positions/velocities, positive masses, rest lengths, stiffnesses, damping, pin set, forces and timestep. Generate rendered vertices from that state; collisions require a separately declared implementation.

For this basic spring example, measure max(L/L0-1) over springs with positive L0 each step and report excursions beyond a declared threshold. Do not claim a hard bound or silently clamp. A separately implemented deformation-projection method must specify its pin handling, iteration policy and residual before claiming constraint enforcement.

Pause preserves particle velocities or clip state. Reset restores initial positions, velocities, rest lengths, pins, parameters and time. Hybrids need explicit ownership/blending instead of two competing writers on the same degree of freedom.
observable_checks: Display-only controls do not imply simulated gravity, stiffness or collision response.
Pinned simulation particles remain at their declared positions, while measured extension is reported independently for the spring families.
Extension above the declared threshold is an observed model discrepancy, not realistic fabric certification. Reset reproduces the initial particle state.

creative_affordances: Stylised garments may stay on bones or use a declared solver; make the chosen model and its actual state inspectable.
Drawing the three spring families in different colours is a free teaching overlay.
known_limits: The selected mass-spring guidance is not a measured textile model; other physical formulations are outside this example.

Provot describes heuristic deformation correction, but this basic implementation only measures stretch. His compared examples omit self-collision; no collision or self-collision implementation is supplied here.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: Provot models cloth as a discrete mass mesh with structural, shear and flexion springs and numerically integrates its dynamics. Concentrated loads can cause unrealistic local extension; increasing stiffness in the discussed explicit integration approach raises computational cost.
claims.scope: Provot1995 discrete graphics model and its discussed integration regime; not a universal cloth formulation or laboratory fabric test.
